title.narrative: Mozambique ACJR 2025

description.narrative: Mozambique faces a compounding humanitarian crisis following three consecutive tropical cyclones—Chido (Dec 2024), Dikeledi (Jan 2025), and most recently Jude—which have devastated communities in Mossuril and Ilha de Moçambique districts. In Ilha de Moçambique, 15,929 households have been affected with 7,586 houses partially damaged, while Mossuril district has seen destruction impacting 43,600 households. The successive disasters have created an emergency where communities struggle with depleted resources and weakened resilience. Critical infrastructure has been compromised: 85 schools are non-functional, agricultural land in Ilha de Moçambique and in Mossuril were flooded, and water systems have been extensively damaged. The recent MIRA identified food as the primary need, while water and sanitation issues pose serious public health risks. The root causes extend beyond the cyclones to include pre-existing vulnerabilities, limited household resilience after previous disasters, inadequate disaster preparedness, and insufficient local response capacity. Without addressing both immediate needs and underlying weaknesses, affected communities face prolonged recovery challenges and heightened vulnerability to future climate shocks.

SUMMARY Tropical Cyclone Jude is the third cyclone to hit Mozambique in three months. Previous cyclones (Chido in Dec 2024, Dikeledi in Jan 2025) caused massive destruction in Cabo Delgado and Nampula. Communities now face compounded challenges: depleted resources, weakened infrastructure, and unaddressed vulnerabilities. Response Plan: Plan and AENA will provide emergency assistance focusing on Food Security and Livelihoods (FSL), Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), and protection mainstreaming. Target Areas: Mossuril and Ilha de Moçambique districts were affected by all three cyclones, with Jude causing the most recent damage. The selection was based on needs assessment and gaps identified through coordination with clusters and other DRA members. Plan and AENA are already active in all eligible districts.

The activity builds on Plan and AENA’s ongoing humanitarian work in Mossuril and Ilha de Moçambique, where both organizations have been operational through multiple crises, including the impacts of three cyclones. It leverages findings from their recent assessments and contributions to the joint Multi-Cluster Initial Rapid Assessment (MIRA). Coordination with clusters and DRA members ensured the activity responds to the most urgent, unmet needs. Other active organizations include WFP, which provided flood impact analysis informing agricultural loss data, and local health and WASH actors addressing immediate post-cyclone needs. However, significant gaps remain in sustained FSL and WASH support with integrated protection. The proposed activity fills a critical gap by combining lifesaving food and water interventions with a longer-term approach to food security and public health resilience, particularly where damage to infrastructure and livelihoods has outpaced the capacity of ongoing responses.

The activity will deliver a rapid, lifesaving Food Security and Livelihoods (FSL) and Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) response with protection mainstreaming, targeting the most affected and vulnerable communities in Mossuril and Ilha de Moçambique. These districts were selected based on joint needs assessments, including the MIRA, consultations with DRA partners and clusters, and Plan and AENA’s operational presence and contextual understanding.
Food Security and Livelihoods (FSL): - Plan and AENA will support 15,000 individuals (approx. 3,000 households) with basic food assistance using a voucher modality. Each household will receive monthly vouchers valued at 5,880 MZN for three months, in line with FSL Cluster guidance. This approach ensures flexibility, dignity, and a boost to local markets. - In parallel, the project will support the restoration of agricultural livelihoods for the most vulnerable households, particularly those that lost crops due to the cyclones. This will be done through the distribution of agricultural input kits (seeds and tools) and targeted agricultural training to enhance resilience and reduce long-term food assistance dependency.
WASH Interventions: In response to the damage to water and sanitation infrastructure and the increased risk of waterborne diseases, the project will:
- Rehabilitate 10 community water points to restore access to safe water. - Construct or rehabilitate sanitation facilities in 10 cyclone-affected schools to promote safe learning environments. - Distribute hygiene and dignity kits to all 15,000 beneficiaries, prioritizing girls and women. - Provide community-based trainings on hygiene promotion and shallow well maintenance/rehabilitation to increase local capacity for managing water needs.
Protection Mainstreaming: Protection will be fully integrated across all activities. This includes: - Conducting community sensitization during distributions to raise awareness on issues such as child protection, safeguarding, and prevention of sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV). - A protection mapping exercise, coordinated with the Protection Cluster, will identify service providers and enable timely referrals for specialized support, particularly to DRA partners Oxfam and Kulima.
Special attention will be paid to high-risk groups such as adolescent girls, female-headed households, and children with disabilities.
Community Participation and Capacity Strengthening: The response follows a community-based approach that prioritizes participation, accountability, and local ownership. Community members will be involved in activity planning, targeting, and implementation processes. Trainings and local engagement will build longer-term capacities, especially in WASH and agriculture, to reduce reliance on external aid.
Implementation Roles and Localisation: While Plan Mozambique will oversee overall project management, reporting, and Monitoring, Evaluation, Research, and Learning (MERL), local partner AENA will be responsible for day-to-day implementation at the community level. AENA will receive 75% of the project budget, including 6% for institutional cost recovery (ICR), and lead the delivery of food assistance, WASH activities, and local coordination. Plan will ensure quality, compliance, and capacity strengthening, with a dedicated team embedded in the implementation zones to work closely with AENA on thematic areas such as the Core Humanitarian Standard (CHS), International Humanitarian Law (IHL), safeguarding, prevention of sexual harassment, exploitation and abuse (PSHEA), and accountability to affected populations (AAP). This will position AENA to access and manage donor funding more independently in the future.
Coordination and Complementarity: Plan and AENA have coordinated closely with other DRA partners and humanitarian actors to avoid duplication and ensure complementarity. This includes alignment with WFP for data on agricultural losses, and coordination with Oxfam and Kulima, particularly around protection. The action was designed jointly with AENA in the lead on activity selection, guided by Plan’s technical inputs and based on continuous coordination with relevant clusters.
In essence, this activity combines immediate, concrete humanitarian relief with the groundwork for greater community resilience and stronger local actor leadership. The food, water, sanitation, and protection components will not only save lives in the short term, but also mitigate the impact of future shocks.

The project targets 15.000 affected people. End beneficiaries are vulnerable children and youth, especially girls, in cyclone-affected households. Priority groups include female-headed households, PLWs, CwDs, and families at risk of CEFM, child labour, or SGBV. The project expects to reach more women than men due to gendered vulnerabilities.
